https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: BIRMINGHAM, England — Nigel Farage dined with business executives Thursday night — and seemed determined not to allow Reform UK’s party conference to be commandeered by a swirling new scandal. But by Friday morning, two of his closest advisers were gone. The loss of Dan Jukes and James Orr to an undercover sting over — yet again — questionable Reform UK donation practices cannot be underestimated. Jukes is known as Farage’s most loyal attack dog — a communications chief who began unflinchingly batting for his boss as a teenager and has lasted for more than a decade in the Farage orbit. They are so close that their relationship is often spoken of as being more like father and son. Orr was Reform’s big policy brain. A Cambridge academic who was leading work to build a robust platform for governance, Orr is a theologian with deep links into the MAGA movement, including a friendship with U.S. Vice President JD Vance. Advertisement Advertisement Aides had billed this get-together of the party faithful as the moment Farage got “ serious ” after a summer dominated by his Clacton by-election battle against comedy candidate Count Binface. That was a fight Farage started himself to try to extinguish separate allegations he had failed to declare millions of pounds in donations from crypto businessman Christopher Harborne. Now fresh headlines in which Farage insists the party has “broken no laws” and denies his team has taken any “dodgy money” are overshadowing the right-wing outfit’s Birmingham gathering. ‘Clandestine projects’ Smoked trout and fillet of beef was on the menu Thursday evening as anxious attendees of the Reform UK business dinner at the National Exhibition Centre watched the Channel 4 footage of the sting on their phones. There was Orr caught on camera arranging potentially rule-breaking funding from a foreign benefactor — via a middle-man in the U.K — to produce favorable polling. There was Jukes discussing “little clandestine projects” that he deems “so valuable” to the party. There was Farage, too, speaking to a fake U.S. donor in his Clacton constituency, appearing to celebrate the great “bang for buck” that the poll — carried in national newspapers with no declaration of its links to Reform UK — had provided. “It worked. Boom ,” Farage said. Advertisement Advertisement Jukes was uncharacteristically not seen at Farage’s side during Thursday night’s dinner. He had been there at his boss’s drinks with political editors shortly before the investigation aired. But his presence on the mind of Reform’s top brass was evident. “The impression over dinner was Nigel was going to back them to the hilt,” said one senior figure in the party who was present at the business event. They were granted anonymity like others in this article to speak frankly about an internal party matter. The argument was that there had been “no law breaking” and that Farage could stand by the embattled duo. “Different combinations of [deputy leader Richard] Tice, Orr etc. were regularly stepping away from tables, having hushed chats in the corners, then coming back,” said a second attendee. “They didn’t acknowledge or mention it to anyone, they certainly weren’t laughing it off.” Meanwhile, there was what one invitee described as a “watch party” of the Channel 4 footage in a hotel room, where senior officials discussed how to handle the situation. At the fifth-floor Sky Bar where many of the conference revelers gathered, senior figures in the party were asking each other “how bad is bad?” over 11.30 p.m. gin and tonics. Most were insistent the row would blow over. If the support for Orr felt more rudimentary, the expectation that Jukes would be fine seemed certain. Advertisement Advertisement “At the bars it was obviously the central topic of conversation, but I don’t think anyone predicted that this morning Orr and Jukes would resign,” the second business dinner attendee said. “The assumption was they would try and brush off and basically fight back, say it’s a hoax etc.” By breakfast there was clarity. Ed Sumner, now indisputably Farage’s most senior communications adviser, spent his birthday morning confirming Jukes and Orr had “stepped down” pending an internal investigation. “The party believes it is important that the investigation is allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice. No further comment will be made while the investigation is ongoing,” read a statement. What prompted the about-turn was unclear, but one senior adviser said Jukes is a “rational thinker,” adding: “When the time was up, he knew the time was up.” The fightback After the defiance over late-night drinks at the Sky Bar, talk of a fightback came at Friday morning’s breakfast buffet. Reform remains neck-and-neck with the governing Labour Party in the polls, and had intended to use Friday to show their readiness for government. “No way is our conference going to get derailed by some stupid posh boy and a Channel 4 investigation,” fumed one of Reform’s gruffer, high-profile champions. Advertisement Advertisement Lee Anderson, who serves as Reform UK’s chief whip, told broadcasters “there’s no chance” of Orr or Jukes coming back — but privately some at the top of the party are holding out for exactly that. The senior figure quoted above predicted the loss of the two aides represented a “tactical retreat” to “take the heat off today” — a “temporary thing,” where an investigation paves the way for a potential return. They also discussed how the party might go on the attack, trying to paint the investigation carried out by journalists at Verbatim, an organization founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, as the work of an “activist.” One Reform MP was overheard reassuring a supporter of Jukes, “It’s alright — we’ll look after him.” Tice, who serves as Farage’s deputy, publicly made the case that Channel 4 itself may have “broken the rules” with an “ entrapment ” operation. But there was no doubt the conference mood had been sullied. “What a sh*tshow,” raged one prospective candidate for Westminster as he joined the long queue into the venue. The senior party figure who spoke of a tactical retreat described Orr as a “very good interlocutor between different people in the party,” a particularly crucial role considering some of the fractures involving Farage’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf. Advertisement Advertisement “He gets on with Nigel, he gets on with Zia. So he would sort of broker stuff,” the figure said of Orr. “It will be a major loss.” Farage’s set-piece conference moment with Jordan Bardella, the president of France’s far-right National Rally party, now comes against the backdrop of scandal. And the scrutiny is unlikely to die down beyond Birmingham. Farage separately expects to be interviewed by parliament’s standards commissioner over the Harborne funding row in the next few weeks. “We clearly need not to create negative headlines that make it harder for people of all stripes [to support us], whether they’re from the respectable tendency or anti-establishment people, who don’t like stories of dodgy money and all that,” the senior party figure said. “It’s bad from all points of view.”

Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP View image in fullscreen Elor Azaria, pictured in an Israeli military court in April 2016, was 20 when he was sentenced. Photograph: Ariel Schalit/AP Israel Israeli president pardons combat medic who shot dead wounded Palestinian attacker Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide country Associated Press in Jerusalem Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.32 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Israel’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attacker who had stabbed a soldier in the occupied West Bank, in a case that divided the country a decade ago. Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter and his release after serving two-thirds of his 18-month sentence drew enormous attention in Israel, where military service is compulsory for most Jewish men. In his first interview after his release, Azaria said he would “act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act”. Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. A mobile phone video captured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head. The office of president Isaac Herzog said in a statement on Saturday that he acted on the recommendation of defence minister Israel Katz. The statement cited the time that had passed, and the spirit of the approaching Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, holiday as among the factors in the decision. This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself | Jonathan Freedland Read more Herzog’s office also said that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, had “expressed his sorrow” in his request. The statement noted that in an earlier request, he called his gunshot an “operational error”. In a separate statement, Katz called it a “right, humane and fitting decision” and said Azaria had been in a “complex operational mission”. But the military’s chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, had said in a letter to the defence minister that the pardon should not be granted, Israeli media reported. The conviction was a rare case of a military court ruling against a soldier for deadly action taken in the field. Top generals had pressed for his prosecution, while many in the Israeli public supported Azaria at a time when there had been a series of stabbings and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. Some supporters protested outside his trial. On Saturday, Israel’s hard-line national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said in a statement that “cancelling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist makes me emotional and very happy”. Some Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria’s sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years. The statement by Herzog’s office on Saturday said that his decision “does not constitute a reassessment of the case”. The divisions over Azaria’s case led to public polling and political pressure that led the defence minister at the time, Moshe Ya’alon, to resign . After the verdict, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for Azaria to be pardoned . After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke”. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Jack Ross, a former Tory local election candidate and CEO of Turning Point UK, was filmed by an undercover reporter discussing the cost of hiring hitmen. Photograph: Guy Corbishley/Alamy View image in fullscreen Jack Ross, a former Tory local election candidate and CEO of Turning Point UK, was filmed by an undercover reporter discussing the cost of hiring hitmen. Photograph: Guy Corbishley/Alamy Conservatives Former Tory candidate suspended over contract killer claims was adviser in Kemi Badenoch’s office Sources close to Tory leader say Jack Ross, who faces party investigation after undercover report, worked as social media consultant Ben Quinn and Jessica Elgot Sun 25 Oct 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 09.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A former Conservative election candidate who was suspended after he was filmed discussing the cost of hiring contract killers worked as a consultant in Kemi Badenoch’s office as recently as last year. Jack Ross is facing an investigation by the Tories after he was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter: “What do you want done?” and apparently offering to “broker” the services of an alleged far-right paramilitary group. Police in Scotland say they will be reviewing an Al Jazeera documentary in which Ross was filmed making a range comments about what a contract killer could be employed to do, and talked about using far-right groups to create disruption on the streets. It has now emerged that he was working in 2025 in the leader of the opposition’s office, which can draw on taxpayer funds to pay staff. By that point, Ross was CEO of Turning Point UK, which was already involving itself in anti-migrant street protests, and listed its chief operating officer as Nick Tenconi, the leader of Ukip. Sources close to Badenoch said Ross was contracted as a junior social media external consultant in her office. However, a Tory staffer familiar with the role of Ross at that time said: “Jack would come and go in the office and a few people raised their eyebrows, but it was brushed under the carpet because he got the party clicks on socials. “He would have been in the same room as Kemi and she would have been aware of him. Some MPs were uncomfortable about it, but senior figures were clear that social media clicks were more important.” Ross was reported by Al Jazeera to have introduced an undercover reporter to a violent criminal from Glasgow with links to the paramilitary Ulster Volunteer Force, who offered to have people killed for money. Al Jazeera approached Ross with a fictitious family problem where a deceased uncle’s business was at risk of being taken over by a gang, whose members were supposedly warned they would “get fucked” if anything happened. Ross replied to this saying: “Yeah, you have to deliver on that as well. You’ve got to explain to me what’s needed … I can then go and broker from there. But I’ve got to say, even to myself … if there’s lashback I’ve got to keep my name out of it.” On another occasion, Ross was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter “What do you want done?” before listing the type of violent options that could be bought. Ross appeared to tell the Al Jazeera journalist: “They can just kick the fuck out of someone. That’s a certain amount. They can start cutting people’s faces up, that’s another amount. And they can stab someone. They can shoot someone. They can kill someone.” Ross, who stood unsuccessfully as a Conservative local election candidate, became CEO of Turning Point UK (TPUK) in 2021, the British offshoot of the US campaign group established by the late rightwing American activist Charlie Kirk. Ross became a fixture of the British rightwing scene, appearing regularly on GB News and joining the conservative thinktank the Bow Group. TPUK was intended to be a campus-based offshoot of the US group and initially endorsed by leading Tory figures such as Priti Patel and Jacob Rees-Mogg. Early members included younger rightwingers such as Tom Harwood, who went on to become a GB News anchor. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion However, it began reinventing itself as a street-protest group after the addition of Tenconi, who has worked closely with Ross, as its COO. Tenconi, as leader of Ukip, has been at the forefont of leading immigration protests in recent years, blending anti-migrant rhetoric with Christian nationalism. Footage released by TPUK last year showed Ross and others from the group meeting Badenoch after Kirk’s death TPUK has not responded to the allegations but Tenconi staged a stunt outside King’s College London on Thursday in an imitation of the campus-based events held by Kirk. A gazebo with TPUK branding was surrounded by students and protesters chanting in opposition. Al Jazeera filmed Tenconi in the company of Ross in 2022 as they discussed the formation of a “new right” which would include the engagement of far-right activists who could cause disruption on the streets, as well as what Tenconi described as the “winning over” of sympathetic MPs. A Tory spokesperson said: “Mr Ross’s membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation. We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing.” Ross and Tenconi have been approached for comment. https://www.dw.com/en/binance-crypto-exc.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OqTg Prefer DW on Google Binance has the largest volume of daily trading out of any crypto platform Image: Silas Stein/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Blockchain analysts said a North Korean hacking unit was likely behind the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals for security checks and said about $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen. US-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as an elite North Korean hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said in a report published Thursday. Why do analysts suspect North Korea? TRM said attackers moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, most of it within about 20 minutes. It described the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," the firm said. Bybit lost $1.5 billion in a hack in February 2025. The FBI attributed that attack to North Korea and TraderTraitor. Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain analysis company Chainalysis, also said the Binance attack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor. What has Binance said about the hack? Binance did not confirm the attribution to North Korea, saying it was "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice." Binance said it worked to secure the affected assets and that it had located and frozen about $3 billion (€2.7 billion) so far. It did not provide information about the remaining $3.3 billion. "Binance will cover all hacking losses," co-founder Yi He said, without providing more details about the incident. "Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a company spokesperson said. Binance said its initial investigation suggested an attacker had compromised a software infrastructure engineer's laptop, gaining access to an internal service and submitting unauthorized withdrawals. The company said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked. The news of the possible hack sent Bitcoin's value tumbling by 3.2% on Thursday evening, dropping below $79,000. Who is Binance ex-CEO Zhao? Zhao, who founded the Binance platform in 2017, said "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered." He stepped down as CEO after pleading guilty in 2023 . to failing to prevent money laundering on his platform. US President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025. Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of cryptocurrency ventures by US President Donald Trump and his family.
